mainTopic: End of perek המוכר את הבית; start of perek המוכר את הספינה: what is sold with a ship, the meaning of its parts, and רבה's sea stories
overview: This amud opens with the last exchange of the perek המוכר את הבית. The גמרא asks why ריש לקיש's ruling was needed if it only matches רבי שמעון, and answers that it shows רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי also holds like רבי שמעון. After the Hadran, a new perek begins with a משנה about selling a ship. The mast, sail, anchors and steering gear go with the ship, but the slaves, packing bags and אנתיקי do not, unless the seller says 'it and everything in it.' The גמרא explains the words תורן, נס, עוגין and מנהיגין, proving each one from a פסוק. A ברייתא then adds the gangway, the water tank and a small boat. רבא explains that ביצית and דוגית are two local names for that same boat. Then the גמרא turns to אגדה: רבה tells sailors' stories about huge waves, and two waves talking about the sand border ה׳ set for the sea. The amud ends as רבה begins a story about the demon הורמין בר לילית, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why not just call this the known dispute?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why ריש לקיש's statement was needed, since it is simply the familiar מחלוקת between רבי שמעון and רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us say this is just the dispute between רבי שמעון and the רבנן!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the previous ruling. It asks why ריש לקיש needed to say it at all, since we already know this exact disagreement between רבי שמעון and רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the גמרא worked out that according to רבי שמעון, even carob and sycamore trees are not included when a field is consecrated. So ריש לקיש's ruling, in the name of רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי, seems to add nothing new. It is just one side of a dispute we already know.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us say: a way of suggesting that something is already known or obvious

phrases.english: But let us say it is the dispute of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis!
phrases.notes: He means: we already know this argument from earlier, so why repeat it as a new statement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the previous daf's discussion of ריש לקיש's ruling about carob and sycamore trees in a consecrated field.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for ריש לקיש's statement in the name of רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling matches רבי שמעון's known view, so stating it seems redundant.

steps.title: It teaches that another Sage holds like רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The statement is needed to show that רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי holds the same view as רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us this: רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי holds like רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The new piece of information is who else holds this view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling itself is not new. What is new is that רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי agrees with רבי שמעון. So רבי שמעון is not alone in this opinion, and that is worth knowing.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us: introduces the new point of a statement

steps.whatToRemember: A statement that seems to repeat a known dispute can still teach something new: which other Sage agrees with one side.

phrases.english: This is what he teaches us:
that Rabbi Menachem son of Rabbi Yosei
holds like Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by pointing out what is new in the statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the new information (which Sage holds the view) rather than a new ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement seemed redundant, since it only repeats רבי שמעון's position.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that רבי מנחם ברבי יוסי agrees with רבי שמעון.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing המוכר את הבית
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the perek המוכר את הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, המוכר את הבית.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the perek about selling a house. A new perek begins right after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Hadran is a traditional farewell said when finishing a perek. It expresses the hope to come back and learn it again. It is not part of the argument.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you: said when finishing a perek

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'One who sells the house'
phrases.notes: 'One who sells the house' is the name of the perek that just ended, taken from its first words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the perek after the final exchange in steps 1-2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The perek המוכר את הבית is complete.

steps.title: Selling a ship: what is included and what is not
steps.stepSummary: The new perek's משנה rules that selling a ship includes the mast, sail, anchors and steering equipment, but not the slaves, the packing bags or the אנתיקי.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sells a ship has sold the mast, the sail, the anchors, and everything that steers it. But he has not sold the slaves, the packing bags, or the אנתיקי.
steps.whatsHappening: A new perek begins with a משנה about selling a ship. It lists which items automatically go along with the ship and which do not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The parts that make the ship work as a ship (mast, sail, anchors, steering gear) are counted as part of it. Things that are only used on the ship or carried by it (slaves, bags, אנתיקי) are separate property. They stay with the seller.

keyTerms.meaning: A ship part (the גמרא explains it as the mast)
A ship part (the גמרא explains it as the sail)
A ship part (the גמרא explains it as the anchors)
The things that steer or drive the ship

phrases.english: One who sells the ship

phrases.aramaic: מָכַר אֶת הַתּוֹרֶן וְאֶת הַנֵּס וְאֶת הָעוֹגִין,
phrases.english: has sold the toren, and the nes, and the ogin,
and all the things that steer it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא מָכַר לֹא אֶת הָעֲבָדִים,
phrases.english: But he has not sold the slaves,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אֶת הַמַּרְצוּפִין, וְלֹא אֶת הָאַנְתִיקֵי.
phrases.english: nor the packing bags, nor the antikei.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the new perek after the Hadran.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ship sale includes its working equipment but not slaves, packing bags or אנתיקי.

steps.title: Saying 'it and everything in it' includes all
steps.stepSummary: If the seller says 'it and all that is in it,' then everything, even the excluded items, is sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he said to him, 'It and everything inside it,' all of them are sold.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a condition. Clear wording from the seller can include the items that are normally left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The default rule follows what the word 'ship' normally covers. When the seller adds 'and everything in it,' he has openly widened the sale. So the slaves, bags and אנתיקי go to the buyer too.

keyTerms.meaning: And when he said to him: introduces a case with special wording

steps.whatToRemember: In a sale, the default is the normal meaning of the word ('ship'). The seller's added words can make the sale wider.

phrases.english: And when he said to him:
'It and all that is inside it,'
then all of them are sold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the exclusions listed in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With the wording 'it and all that is in it,' even the normally excluded items are sold.

steps.title: תורן means the mast
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains תורן as the mast and brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: תורן is the mast. And so it says: 'They took cedars from Lebanon to make a mast for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the hard words in the משנה. It starts with תורן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא translates תורן into Aramaic as איסקריא, the mast. A פסוק about building a ship uses the same word for wood made into a mast. That confirms the meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says: introduces a supporting פסוק

phrases.english: GEMARA: 'Toren' is the mast.
And so it says:
'They took cedars from Lebanon
to make a mast for you.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא's explanation of the משנה's terms from step 4.

steps.title: נס means the sail
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains נס as the sail and brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: נס is the sail. And so it says: 'Fine embroidered linen from Egypt was your sail, to be for you a נס.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next word in the משנה, נס, and explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נס is translated as אדרא, the sail. The פסוק describes a ship's spread-out linen as its נס. That shows נס means the sail.

phrases.english: 'Nes' is the sail.
And so it says:
'Fine linen with embroidery from Egypt
was what you spread out, to be a sail for you.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues defining the משנה's ship terms, same pattern as step 6.

steps.title: עוגין means the anchors
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא teaches that עוגין are the ship's anchors, proved from a פסוק in רות where the same root means being held back in one place.
steps.simpleTranslation: עוגין: רבי חייא taught, these are its anchors. And so it says: 'Would you wait for them until they grow up? Would you hold yourselves back for them and not marry a man?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third word, עוגין, using a teaching of רבי חייא and a פסוק from רות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, נעמי asks if her daughters-in-law will stay tied down, unmarried, waiting. The root ע-ג-נ means being held fixed in place. An anchor does exactly that to a ship.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught (introduces a teaching of a תנא)
You would hold yourselves back (stay tied down)

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא proves the ship words of the משנה (תורן, נס, עוגין) from פסוקים that use the same words.

phrases.english: 'Ogin': Rabbi Chiya taught:
These are its anchors.
And so it says:
'Would you wait for them until they grow up?
Would you hold yourselves back for them and not be married to a man?'
phrases.notes: The key word is תעגנה, the same root as עוגין: being held in one place, like an anchor holds a ship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues defining the משנה's ship terms, now with a teaching of רבי חייא.

steps.title: מנהיגין are the ship's oars
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא explains that the משנה's word מנהיגין means the ship's oars and brings a פסוק from יחזקאל as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: The 'steering equipment' in the משנה means the oars. The פסוק says: 'Of the oaks of Bashan they made your oars.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps defining the words of the משנה, and now explains מנהיגין as the oars that steer and move the ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the earlier steps for תורן, נס and עוגין, the גמרא pairs a hard word in the משנה with a פסוק. Here the פסוק shows that oars are a normal, built-in part of a ship, so they belong to the ship and are sold with it.

keyTerms.meaning: בשן, a region known for its oak trees

phrases.english: "Steering equipment": Rabbi Abba said:
These are its oars.
And so it says:
"Of the oaks of Bashan they made your oars."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word definitions of the משנה's ship parts (after תורן, נס, עוגין).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מנהיגין in the משנה means the ship's oars.

steps.title: A second פסוק showing oars belong to ships
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another פסוק as proof that מנהיגין are oars: sailors 'holding the oar' come down from their ships.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you like, prove it from this פסוק: 'And all who hold the oar shall come down from their ships.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, alternate proof for the same definition of מנהיגין as oars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not change the definition; מנהיגין are still the oars. It only offers a different פסוק from יחזקאל as the source. Here the sailors who leave their ships are described as 'all who hold the oar.'

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another option
Those who hold the oar (the rowers)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say it is from here:
"And they shall come down from their ships,
all who hold the oar."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate proof for the same definition from step 9.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists more items sold with a ship
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the gangway and water tank are sold with a ship. רבי נתן adds the ביצית and סומכוס adds the דוגית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Someone who sells a ship has also sold the gangway and the water tank inside it. רבי נתן says he has sold the ביצית. סומכוס says he has sold the דוגית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds more things that are automatically included when a ship is sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed mast, sail, anchors and oars. The ברייתא adds the gangway for boarding and the ship's water supply. Then two תנאים each add a small boat, using two different words, which sets up the next step's question of whether they really disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
Gangway, the board used to get on and off the ship
Water tank (drinking water stored on the ship)
A small boat attached to the ship (רבי נתן's word)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who sells the ship
has sold the gangway,
and the water tank that is inside it.
Rabbi Natan says:

phrases.aramaic: הַמּוֹכֵר אֶת הַסְּפִינָה – מָכַר אֶת הַבִּיצִּית.
phrases.english: One who sells the ship has sold the bitzit.
Sumakhos says:

phrases.aramaic: הַמּוֹכֵר אֶת הַסְּפִינָה – מָכַר אֶת הַדּוּגִית.
phrases.english: One who sells the ship has sold the dugit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defining the משנה's words to a ברייתא that adds more items included in the sale.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a ship includes the gangway and water tank; רבי נתן and סומכוס also include a small boat (ביצית / דוגית).

steps.title: ביצית and דוגית are the same boat
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that רבי נתן and סומכוס do not disagree. They mean the same small boat, but each uses the word from where he lived.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: ביצית is the same as דוגית. רבי נתן was from בבל, where people say 'the small boats of Meishan.' סומכוס was from ארץ ישראל and used the word from the פסוק 'and your remnant in fishing boats.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא clears up what looks like an argument between רבי נתן and סומכוס by showing they are using two local words for one thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without רבא, we might think the two תנאים include two different boats. רבא shows it is only a difference in language: a Babylonian word against a word taken from a פסוק used in ארץ ישראל. So the הלכה is the same for both: the ship's small boat is sold with it.

keyTerms.meaning: As people say: proof from common speech

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an argument about which boat is sold. רבא shows both תנאים agree; only their words are different.
steps.whatToRemember: When a ship is sold, its small attached boat goes with it. ביצית and דוגית are two names for that same boat.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Bitzit is the same as dugit.
Rabbi Natan was a Babylonian,
so he calls it "butzit,"
as people say:
"The small boats of Meishan."
Sumakhos was from Eretz Yisrael,
so he calls it "dugit,"
as it is written:
"And your remnant in fishing boats."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two different words in the ברייתא of step 11 and shows there is no real argument.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ביצית and דוגית mean the same small boat; the difference is only Babylonian versus ארץ ישראל language.

steps.title: רבה's sailors tell of a wave calmed by holy names
steps.stepSummary: רבה reports that sailors told him a ship-sinking wave has a white fiery streak at its top, and they calm it by striking it with clubs engraved with names of ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Sailors told me that the wave that sinks ships looks like it has a streak of white fire on top. We hit it with clubs engraved with 'אהיה אשר אהיה, יה, ה׳ צבאות, אמן אמן סלה,' and it calms down.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the topic is ships, the גמרא begins a series of stories that רבה heard from sailors. This is the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a הלכה about selling. It is אגדה connected to the ship theme. The sailors describe how to spot the dangerous wave (the white fire at its head) and how the holy names engraved on their clubs make it stop.

keyTerms.meaning: Seafarers (literally, 'those who go down to the sea')
A streak or ray of fire

steps.confusionAlert: This is רבה (with a ה), a different אמורא from רבא (with an א) in the previous step.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Seafarers told me:
This wave that sinks a ship
looks like a streak of fire
that is white, at its head,
and we strike it with clubs
that have engraved on them:
"I will be what I will be, Yah, ה׳ of Hosts,
amen, amen, selah,"
and it calms down.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה אִשְׁתַּעוּ לִי נָחוֹתֵי יַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the halacha of selling a ship to a series of sea stories connected by the ship theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ship-sinking wave marked by white fire is calmed by striking it with clubs engraved with names of ה׳.

steps.title: Sailors describe the enormous size of the waves
steps.stepSummary: רבה reports that sailors told him waves are 300 פרסאות apart and 300 פרסאות high. Once a wave lifted them so high that they saw a small star up close, and any higher would have burned them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Sailors told me that the distance between one wave and the next is 300 פרסאות, and a wave is 300 פרסאות high. Once, while we were traveling, a wave lifted us so high that we saw the resting place of a small star. It looked as big as a field where you could plant forty measures of mustard seed. If the wave had lifted us any higher, the star's heat would have burned us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the series of sea stories in the name of רבה. This one is about how huge and powerful the ocean's waves are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 was about a dangerous wave and how sailors calm it. Now רבה adds what sailors told him about the size of the waves. The point of the story is how gigantic they are: they rise high enough to reach close to the stars.

keyTerms.meaning: פרסאות, a long measure of distance

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה, אִשְׁתַּעוּ לִי נָחוֹתֵי יַמָּא:
phrases.english: Rabba said: Seafarers told me:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין גַּלָּא לְגַלָּא תְּלָת מְאָה פַּרְסֵי,
phrases.english: Between one wave and the next wave there are three hundred parasangs,
and the height of a wave is three hundred parasangs.
Once we were traveling on our way,
and a wave lifted us up

phrases.aramaic: עַד דַּחֲזֵינַן בֵּי מַרְבַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּכוֹכְבָא זוּטָא,
phrases.english: until we saw the resting place of a small star,
and it seemed to me as large as an area for sowing
forty se'a of mustard seed.
And if it had lifted us any higher,
we would have been burned by its heat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה, אִשְׁתַּעוּ לִי נָחוֹתֵי יַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another sailors' report by רבה, continuing the series of sea stories from step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ocean waves are enormously tall and far apart. One lifted a ship close enough to a star that going higher would have burned it.

steps.title: One wave asks another what is left to destroy
steps.stepSummary: Continuing the story, one wave calls to another asking if anything in the world is left to wash away. The other answers that even a thin line of sand stops it, because ה׳ made sand the sea's border, as the פסוק in ירמיהו says.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one wave called out to its friend: 'My friend, did you leave anything in the world that you didn't wash away, so that I can come and destroy it?' The other wave answered: 'Go out and see the power of your Master. Even a thread's width of sand, I cannot pass it.' As it says: 'Will you not fear Me, says ה׳? Will you not tremble before Me, Who placed sand as the border of the sea, a law forever that it cannot cross?'
steps.whatsHappening: The story goes on: the waves 'talk' to each other. The second wave explains that ה׳ has set a limit the sea cannot cross.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first wave shows the sea's wild power and desire to destroy. The second wave answers that all that power stops at a thin strip of sand, because ה׳ commanded it. The פסוק from ירמיהו proves that the sand is ה׳'s permanent border for the sea.

keyTerms.meaning: Sand as thin as a thread

steps.whatToRemember: The waves are huge and powerful, but ה׳ set the sand as a limit the sea can never cross.

phrases.english: And the wave raised its voice to its friend:
"My friend, did you leave anything in the world
that you did not wash away,
so that I may come and destroy it?"
It said to it: "Go out and see the power of your Master,
even a thread's width of sand, I cannot cross it,
as it says: 'Will you not fear Me, says ה׳,
will you not tremble before Me,
Who placed sand as the border of the sea,
a law forever, which it cannot cross?'"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same sailors' story about the giant waves, now adding a conversation between two waves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: However strong the sea is, it cannot cross the sand border ה׳ set for it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns a story about the sea's size into a lesson about ה׳'s control over even the mightiest forces.

steps.title: רבה saw a demon running on the city wall
steps.stepSummary: רבה begins a new story: he saw the demon הורמין בר לילית running along the top of the wall of מחוזא, and a rider on horseback below could not catch him. Then a story starts about two mules saddled for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: I myself saw הורמין, the son of לילית, running along the top of the wall of the city מחוזא. A horseman riding below him chased him but could not catch up. Once, people saddled two mules for him, and they were standing...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story in the name of רבה, this time something he saw himself. The story about the mules is only beginning here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, רבה repeated what sailors told him. Now he says 'I myself saw' a demon who moved faster than a rider on horseback. The last line sets up the next part of the story about two mules.

keyTerms.meaning: הורמין, son of לילית, a demon
On the top edges of the wall

phrases.english: Rabba said: I myself saw
Hurmin, son of Lilith,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָא רָהֵיט אַקּוּפְיָא דְּשׁוּרָא דְמָחוֹזָא,
phrases.english: when he was running on the top edges of the wall of Meḥoza,

phrases.aramaic: וְרָהֵיט פָּרָשָׁא כִּי רְכִיב חֵיוְתָא מִתַּתָּאֵיהּ,
phrases.english: and a horseman riding an animal raced below him,
but could not catch up to him.
Once, they saddled for him
two mules, and they were standing

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from sailors' reports about the sea to a new story רבה saw himself, about a demon in מחוזא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה saw the demon הורמין בר לילית run along the top of the wall of מחוזא faster than a rider on horseback.
